passage:
Yamini's sketchbook was hidden under the mattress again. Papa had found it last month and said, very quietly, "Science, Yamini. Or don't call yourself our daughter. What will the family say if you draw cartoons for a living?"
He wasn't shouting. He never shouted. He paid for her tuition, sat up with her before exams, brought her favourite jalebis every Friday. That was what made it so confusing.
On the building terrace, she showed a new drawing to Yusuf, who lived two floors down and was in his first year of design college.
"It's really good," he said. "Why do you look scared?"
"Because I love them," Yamini said. "And every time I pick up a pencil, it feels like I'm choosing to lose them."
Yusuf didn't tell her what to do. He only said, "Maybe the school counsellor could help you talk to them. You shouldn't have to carry this alone."

qa.a: It was hidden under the mattress again.

qa.q: Why does picking up a pencil feel like losing them to Yamini?
qa.a: She loves them deeply, and Papa's warning made drawing feel like choosing to be cut off, so love and freedom pull against each other.

qa.q: What small step could help Yamini now?
qa.a: She could take up Yusuf's idea and ask the school counsellor to help her talk to Papa and the family, so she isn't carrying the pressure alone.

qa.q: How might Papa see his warning about science?
qa.a: He probably sees it as care and duty, protecting her future and the family's name, without noticing how frightening the threat feels to her.

grounding: A girl whose loving father threatens shame and disowning over her wish to draw feels torn between love and freedom.

"Where were you till six?" Madhuri asked, not looking up from the rotis.
"At Neha's. Project work, Amma."
"I told you. That girl is a distraction. People talk."
"Neha's my best friend. What people?"
"Your aunties. Your grandmother. You want them saying I raised a girl who roams around?" Amma finally looked up. "If you go there again, don't expect me to fight for your hostel next year."
Vidya's throat tightened. "That's not fair."
"Fair?" Amma's voice softened. "I lie awake worrying every night. I do everything for you. This is for your own good, kanna."
Vidya stood there, torn. Amma's hands were floury, her eyes tired and full of love. Vidya wanted to hug her. She also wanted to scream.
"Okay," she said. She went to her room and texted Neha: can't come tmrw. sorry. will explain.
Then she sat on the bed, not sure what she would explain.

qa.q: Whose house was Vidya at until six?
qa.a: Vidya was at Neha's house, doing project work.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she stood there?
qa.a: She felt torn, wanting to hug Amma for her tired, loving eyes and also wanting to scream at the unfair threat.

qa.q: What could Vidya do after texting Neha?
qa.a: She could talk to a trusted adult outside the argument, like a school counsellor, about how to speak calmly with Amma about her friendship.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see her own rule?
qa.a: Madhuri sees it as worry and love, for Vidya's own good, shaped by fear of what relatives will say, not as control.

grounding: A girl whose loving mother threatens to withdraw support if she keeps seeing her best friend feels torn between love and freedom.
